learner:
Beginner-intermediate guitarist who plays by ear; knows open chords and some barre chords; cannot read notation.
Goal: understand enough theory to write original chord progressions.
Can name the notes of C major; guessed correctly that a key has seven chords but cannot explain why.
Does not know what makes a chord minor, so intervals and chord construction are the main gaps.

lessons.title: Half Steps and Whole Steps on the Fretboard
lessons.objective: Measure the distance between notes in half and whole steps using frets.
lessons.hook: Every scale and chord is built from these two step sizes, and your fretboard already shows them.
lessons.explain: A half step is one fret on the guitar. A whole step is two half steps, or two frets. For example, going up from C you pass C, then C#, then D: two half steps, so C to D is a whole step. There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher. Among the natural notes, E to F and B to C are half steps, with no sharp between them; other neighbouring natural notes are whole steps.
key_facts: A half step is one fret on the guitar.
A whole step is two half steps, or two frets.
There are 12 different notes before the pattern repeats an octave higher.
E to F and B to C are half steps; other neighbouring natural notes are whole steps.

predict.q: The open low string is E. What note is at the 1st fret?

angles: Think of the 12 notes as a clock: each fret moves one hour, and two frets move two hours. Only E–F and B–C sit right next to each other with no black-key note between.
On a piano, a half step is any key to the very next key, black or white. E–F and B–C are the two places where white keys touch with no black key between them.
claims: One guitar fret equals one half step.
A whole step equals two half steps.
Western music uses 12 distinct pitch classes.
E–F and B–C are the only half steps between neighbouring natural notes.

items.q: On guitar, moving up one fret raises a note by:
items.why: Each fret is the smallest step, one half step.
misconceptions: Believes one fret equals two half steps
Believes one fret spans three half steps
Believes one fret jumps a full octave

items.q: You play a note at the 5th fret. A whole step higher on the same string is at:
items.why: A whole step is two frets, so 5 + 2 = 7.
misconceptions: Believes a whole step is one fret
Believes a whole step is three frets
Believes a whole step is five frets

items.q: Which pair of natural notes is only a half step apart?
items.why: B–C has no sharp between it, so it is a half step.
misconceptions: Believes C and D have no note between them
Believes F and G have no note between them
Believes A and B have no note between them

items.q: How many different notes are there before the pattern repeats an octave higher?
items.why: Counting every fret, there are 12 different notes before the octave.
misconceptions: Confuses notes in a major scale with all available notes
Counts the octave note as a new note
Believes some sharps are missing from the set

items.q: Name the two pairs of neighbouring natural notes that have no sharp or flat between them.
accept: E and F, B and C
items.why: These are the only natural-note pairs a half step apart.

items.q: A is at the 5th fret of the low E string. At which fret is the note a whole step higher, and what is that note?
items.why: A whole step is two frets, and A to B is a whole step.

lessons.title: Building Any Major Scale
lessons.objective: Build the major scale starting from any note using the step pattern.
lessons.hook: A key is just a major scale, so once you can build any scale you can find chords in any key.
lessons.explain: Every major scale follows the pattern W W H W W W H (whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half). Start on any note and apply it. C major uses only natural notes, C D E F G A B, because its half steps fall exactly at E–F and B–C. For example, G major: G (W) A (W) B (H) C (W) D (W) E (W) F# (H) G. G major has one sharp, F#, needed to keep the pattern. A major scale has seven different notes before the octave.
key_facts: The major scale pattern is W W H W W W H.
C major uses only natural notes: C D E F G A B.
G major has one sharp, F#.
A major scale has seven different notes before the octave.

predict.q: Besides F#, which other note in D major needs a sharp?

angles: Picture the pattern as two groups of fret jumps on one string: 2, 2, 1, then 2, 2, 2, 1. Play it from any fret and you hear 'do re mi fa sol la ti do'.
C major is the template: its natural notes already fit W W H W W W H. Other keys add sharps or flats wherever a note must move to keep the same gaps.

rungs.text: D major: D (W) E (W) F# (H) G (W) A (W) B (W) C# (H) D. Two sharps, F# and C#, keep the pattern.
A major: A (W) B (W) __ (H) D (W) E (W) __ (W) __ (H) A. Fill in the three missing notes.
Build F major from scratch using W W H W W W H.

claims: The major scale step pattern is W W H W W W H.
C major contains no sharps or flats.
G major contains one sharp, F#.
D major contains F# and C#.
A major scale has seven distinct notes.

items.q: Which is the major scale step pattern?
options: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
W W W H W W H
H W W W H W W
items.answer: W W H W W W H
items.why: The half steps fall after the 3rd and 7th notes.
misconceptions: Confuses the major pattern with the natural minor pattern
Places the first half step after the 4th note
Believes the scale starts with a half step

items.q: Which note in G major is sharp?
items.why: E to F is only a half step, so F is raised to F# to make the whole step the pattern needs.
misconceptions: Confuses G major with D major
Believes the key note itself is sharpened
Believes a sharp falls on the fifth note

items.q: How many different notes are in a major scale before the octave?
items.why: The 8th note is the starting note repeated an octave higher.
misconceptions: Counts the octave as a new note
Confuses the major scale with a pentatonic scale
Confuses a scale with all 12 notes

items.q: Why does C major need no sharps or flats?
options: Its half steps land on E–F and B–C
C is the lowest note in music
Natural notes are all whole steps apart
items.answer: Its half steps land on E–F and B–C
items.why: The pattern's half steps match the natural half steps exactly.
misconceptions: Believes C has a special position as the lowest pitch
Believes sharps belong only to minor scales
Forgets E–F and B–C are half steps

items.q: Using the pattern, what is the 3rd note of D major?
items.why: D to E is a whole step, and E to F# is a whole step.

items.q: Write the notes of the C major scale.
items.answer: C D E F G A B
accept: C D E F G A B C
items.why: C major uses only natural notes.

lessons.title: Thirds and Fifths
lessons.objective: Find the major third, minor third and perfect fifth above any note.
lessons.hook: These three intervals are the building blocks of every basic chord.
lessons.explain: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps. Three intervals build every basic chord. A major third is 4 half steps: C to E, four frets. A minor third is 3 half steps: C to Eb, three frets. A perfect fifth is 7 half steps: C to G. On guitar, from any note count up 4 frets for its major third, 3 for its minor third, and 7 for its fifth.
key_facts: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps.
A major third is 4 half steps.
A minor third is 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth is 7 half steps.
angles: Measure with frets on one string: 3 frets up is a minor third, 4 frets up is a major third, and 7 frets up is a fifth, the same gap as a power chord.
A minor third is just a major third shrunk by one fret. Both span three letter names, C–D–E, but they differ in size by one half step.
claims: A major third spans 4 half steps.
A minor third spans 3 half steps.
A perfect fifth spans 7 half steps.
C to E is a major third and C to G is a perfect fifth.

items.q: How many half steps are in a major third?
items.why: A major third is 4 half steps, such as C to E.
misconceptions: Confuses a major third with a minor third
Confuses a major third with a perfect fourth
Confuses a major third with a whole step

items.q: What note is a minor third above C?
items.why: Three half steps above C is Eb.
misconceptions: Confuses a minor third with a major third
Believes a minor third is a whole step
Believes a minor third is 5 half steps

items.q: What note is a perfect fifth above A?
items.why: Seven half steps above A is E.
misconceptions: Counts 5 half steps, a perfect fourth
Counts 8 half steps
Counts 10 half steps

items.q: An interval is:
items.why: An interval measures the gap between two notes in half steps.
misconceptions: Confuses an interval with a triad
Confuses an interval with note duration
Confuses an interval with tempo

items.q: What note is a major third above G?
items.why: Four half steps above G (G#, A, A#, B) is B.

items.q: Starting from the same note, how far apart are the major third and the minor third?
items.answer: One half step; the minor third is one fret lower.
items.why: A major third is 4 half steps and a minor third is 3.

lessons.title: What Makes a Chord Major or Minor
lessons.objective: Spell major and minor triads and explain the difference between them.
lessons.hook: Knowing why Em sounds sad and E sounds bright lets you choose the moods in your progressions.
lessons.explain: A triad is a root, a third and a fifth. A major triad has a major third (4 half steps) and a perfect fifth above the root, so C major is C–E–G. A minor triad has a minor third (3 half steps) and a perfect fifth, so C minor is C–Eb–G. The only difference is the third: lowering it one half step turns major into minor. For example, going from open E to Em, you lift the finger fretting G#, so the third drops to G.
key_facts: A triad is a root, a third and a fifth.
A major triad has a major third and a perfect fifth above the root.
A minor triad has a minor third and a perfect fifth above the root.
The only difference is the third, lowered one half step for minor.
fixes: Did not know what makes a chord minor.

predict.q: How many notes differ between A major and A minor?

angles: Compare A and Am open shapes: A has C# on the B string's 2nd fret, while Am fingers C on the 1st fret. That single fret is the whole difference.
Think root and fifth as a power chord, the frame. The third fills in the colour: 4 half steps up sounds bright (major), 3 half steps sounds dark (minor).
claims: A triad contains a root, third and fifth.
C major is C–E–G and C minor is C–Eb–G.
A minor chord has a minor third above the root.
E major contains G# and E minor contains G.

items.q: What makes a chord minor?
options: Its third is a minor third above the root
Its fifth is lowered one half step
It has four notes instead of three
Its root is a flat note
items.answer: Its third is a minor third above the root
items.why: A minor triad's third is 3 half steps above the root.
misconceptions: Confuses minor with diminished
Believes adding a note makes a chord minor
Believes flat roots make chords minor

items.q: To turn A major (A–C#–E) into A minor, change:
items.why: Lowering the third one half step makes the chord minor.
misconceptions: Believes the root is lowered for minor
Believes the fifth is lowered for minor
Believes the fifth is raised for minor

items.q: Which notes form a G major triad?
items.why: B is a major third above G, and D is a perfect fifth.
misconceptions: Spells G minor instead of G major
Uses a fourth instead of a third
Lowers the fifth instead of keeping it perfect

items.q: A triad contains:
options: a root, a third and a fifth
a root, a fourth and a sixth
any three notes of a scale
items.answer: a root, a third and a fifth
items.why: A triad stacks a third and a fifth on a root.
misconceptions: Confuses the triad with other stackings
Believes any three notes make a triad
Confuses a triad with octave doublings

items.q: Spell a D minor triad.
items.why: F is a minor third above D, and A is a perfect fifth.

items.q: Going from open E to Em, you lift one finger. Which chord tone changes, and how?
items.answer: The third: G# drops a half step to G.
accept: the third lowers from G# to G
items.why: Lowering the third one half step makes the chord minor.

lessons.title: The Diminished Triad
lessons.objective: Spell a diminished triad and recognise its symbol.
lessons.hook: One chord in every major key is diminished, so you need it to complete the set.
lessons.explain: A diminished triad is a root, a minor third and a diminished fifth. A diminished fifth is 6 half steps, one less than a perfect fifth. For example, B diminished is B–D–F: B to D is 3 half steps and D to F is 3, so B to F is 6. It is written with a small circle, B°. It sounds tense and unstable, wanting to move to another chord.
key_facts: A diminished triad is a root, a minor third and a diminished fifth.
A diminished fifth is 6 half steps.
B diminished is B–D–F.
A diminished triad is written with a small circle, as in B°.
angles: Start from a minor triad and lower the fifth by one fret: Bm (B–D–F#) becomes B° (B–D–F).
Stack two minor thirds: B up 3 frets is D, D up 3 frets is F. Two small steps make the squeezed, tense sound.
claims: A diminished triad has a minor third and a diminished fifth.
A diminished fifth spans 6 half steps.
B diminished is spelled B–D–F.
Diminished chords are marked with °.

items.q: How many half steps are in a diminished fifth?
items.why: A diminished fifth is one half step smaller than a perfect fifth of 7.
misconceptions: Confuses a diminished fifth with a perfect fifth
Confuses a diminished fifth with a perfect fourth
Confuses diminished with augmented

items.q: Which notes form B diminished?
items.why: D is a minor third above B, and F is a diminished fifth.
misconceptions: Spells B major instead
Spells B minor instead
Believes diminished keeps a major third

items.q: Which symbol marks a diminished chord?
items.why: The small circle means diminished.
misconceptions: Confuses diminished with minor
Confuses diminished with augmented
Confuses diminished with major

items.q: How does a diminished triad differ from a minor triad on the same root?
options: Its fifth is one half step lower
Its third is one half step higher
Its root is one half step lower
It has an extra fourth note
items.answer: Its fifth is one half step lower
items.why: Both have a minor third, but diminished has a 6-half-step fifth.
misconceptions: Confuses diminished with major
Believes the root moves
Believes diminished adds a note

items.q: Name the three parts of a diminished triad.
items.answer: A root, a minor third and a diminished fifth.
items.why: Those three notes define the diminished triad.

items.q: What note is a diminished fifth above E?
items.why: Six half steps above E is Bb (also called A#).

lessons.title: The Seven Chords in a Key
lessons.objective: List the seven chords that belong to any major key.
lessons.hook: These seven chords are your palette: any of them will sound like they belong in the song.
lessons.explain: A key's chords are built only from its scale notes, by stacking every other note on each scale degree: in C, C–E–G, D–F–A, E–G–B, and so on. The seven scale notes give seven diatonic chords. The pattern of qualities is always major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished. So in C major the chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°. These seven chords sound like they belong together.
key_facts: A key's chords are built from its scale notes by stacking every other note.
The seven scale notes give seven diatonic chords.
The pattern is major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
The chords of C major are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.
fixes: Guessed that a key has seven chords without knowing why.

predict.q: In the key of C, what quality is the chord built on D (D–F–A)?

angles: Skip-a-letter rule: on each letter of the scale take that letter, skip one, take one, skip one, take one. In C, from E you get E–G–B, which is Em because G is 3 half steps above E.
Memorise the shape of the pattern, 'M m m M M m dim', then just write the key's scale and stamp the pattern on it.

rungs.text: Key of G: scale G A B C D E F#. Apply M m m M M m dim: G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em, F#°.
Key of D: scale D E F# G A B C#. Chords: D, __, F#m, G, __, Bm, C#°.
List the seven chords in the key of A major.

claims: Diatonic triads are built by stacking scale notes in thirds.
A major key has seven diatonic triads.
Major-key triad qualities are major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
C major's diatonic chords are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am, B°.

items.q: Why does a major key have seven chords?
options: One triad is built on each of seven scale notes
Guitar has seven easy chord shapes
Every song uses exactly seven chords
Seven is the number of sharps allowed
items.answer: One triad is built on each of seven scale notes
items.why: Each scale degree gives one diatonic triad.
misconceptions: Believes chords in a key come from guitar shapes
Believes songs must use every chord
Confuses chord count with key signatures

items.q: In a major key, what quality is the chord on the 6th degree?
items.why: The pattern's sixth entry is minor.
misconceptions: Misremembers the quality pattern
Confuses the 6th degree with the 7th
Believes augmented chords occur in major keys

items.q: Which chord belongs to the key of C major?
items.why: The ii chord in C is D minor.
misconceptions: Believes every scale note gets a major chord
Forgets C major has G, not G#
Forgets C major has A, not Ab

items.q: Stacking every other scale note on F in C major gives:
items.why: From F, take F, skip G, take A, skip B, take C.
misconceptions: Uses neighbouring notes instead of skipping
Uses a note not in C major
Stacks a fourth instead of a third

items.q: State the quality pattern of chords in a major key, from the 1st degree to the 7th.
items.answer: Major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
accept: M m m M M m dim
items.why: This pattern holds in every major key.

items.q: Why is the chord on E minor in the key of C, not major?
items.answer: C major has G, not G#, and E to G is a minor third.
accept: Because G is 3 half steps above E
items.why: Using only scale notes gives E–G–B, which has a minor third.

lessons.title: Roman Numeral Chord Names
lessons.objective: Name chords by Roman numeral and convert numerals into chords in a key.
lessons.hook: Numerals let you think in patterns that work in every key, which is how songwriters plan progressions.
lessons.explain: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree, so a progression works in any key. Uppercase means major and lowercase means minor; lowercase with ° means diminished. In a major key the chords are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°. For example, in C, I is C, IV is F, V is G and vi is Am, so 'I–IV–V' in C is C–F–G.
key_facts: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree.
Uppercase means major and lowercase means minor.
Lowercase with ° means diminished.
In a major key the chords are I, ii, iii, IV, V, vi, vii°.
angles: Numerals work like the Nashville number system: 'one-four-five' tells any band what to play, whatever key the singer needs.
Count up the scale from the key note: the 1st is I, the 2nd is ii, and so on. The case of the numeral just tells you major or minor.
claims: Roman numerals represent scale degrees.
Uppercase numerals indicate major chords and lowercase indicate minor.
° indicates a diminished chord.
Major-key diatonic numerals are I ii iii IV V vi vii°.

items.q: In a major key, 'ii' means:
options: a minor chord on the second degree
a major chord on the second degree
the second chord played in the song
items.answer: a minor chord on the second degree
items.why: Lowercase means minor, and the numeral gives the degree.
misconceptions: Ignores what lowercase means
Confuses scale degree with song order
Believes the numeral counts notes

items.q: In the key of C, the V chord is:
items.why: G is the 5th degree of C, and V is uppercase, so major.
misconceptions: Believes V is minor
Counts to the 4th degree
Confuses V with vii°

items.q: What does vii° mean?
options: a diminished chord on the seventh degree
a seventh chord on any degree
a minor chord with added seventh
a major chord on the seventh degree
items.answer: a diminished chord on the seventh degree
items.why: ° marks diminished, and vii names the 7th degree.
misconceptions: Confuses the degree number with a seventh chord
Confuses ° with an added seventh
Ignores the lowercase and the °

items.q: Which list gives the correct numerals for a major key?
options: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
I II III IV V VI VII
i ii iii iv v vi vii
I ii III IV v vi VII
items.answer: I ii iii IV V vi vii°
items.why: The numerals follow the major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished pattern.
misconceptions: Believes every chord in a key is major
Believes every chord in a key is minor
Misremembers the quality pattern

items.q: Why do songwriters use Roman numerals instead of chord letters?
items.answer: Numerals name chords by scale degree, so the same progression works in any key.
accept: so a progression can be moved to any key
items.why: Numerals describe chord positions relative to the key.

items.q: In the key of C, which chords are vi and IV?
items.answer: vi is Am and IV is F.
items.why: A is the 6th degree (minor) and F is the 4th (major).

lessons.title: Tonic, Subdominant and Dominant
lessons.objective: Explain the role each chord plays in creating tension and release.
lessons.hook: Progressions feel like stories because chords have jobs: home, away and tension.
lessons.explain: Chords have jobs called functions. The tonic, I, is home: stable, it sounds finished. Dominant chords, V and vii°, create tension that pulls back to I. Subdominant chords, IV and ii, move away from home and often lead to V. Chords sharing notes can share a function: vi (Am in C: A–C–E) shares two notes with I (C–E–G), so it can substitute for I. Example in C: C (home) → F (away) → G (tension) → C (resolved).
key_facts: The tonic, I, is home: stable, it sounds finished.
Dominant chords, V and vii°, create tension that pulls back to I.
Subdominant chords, IV and ii, move away from home and often lead to V.
vi shares two notes with I, so it can substitute for I.

predict.q: Strum C–F–G in the key of C and stop on G. How does it feel?
options: no different from stopping on C

angles: Think of a journey: I is your house, IV and ii are the road out, V is standing at your front door, and returning to I is walking in.
Shared notes explain substitutes: Am (A–C–E) contains C and E from C major, so it feels close to home but with a darker colour.
claims: The I chord has tonic function.
V and vii° have dominant function and tend to resolve to I.
IV and ii have subdominant function and often lead to V.
In C major, Am and C share the notes C and E.

items.q: Which chord most strongly wants to resolve to I?
items.why: V is the dominant, which creates tension pulling to I.
misconceptions: Confuses subdominant with dominant
Believes the tonic substitute pulls to I
Believes iii is the main tension chord

items.q: What function does the ii chord have?
items.why: ii, like IV, moves away from home and leads to V.
misconceptions: Believes minor chords act as home
Believes ii pulls straight back to I
Believes only I, IV and V have functions

items.q: Why can Am substitute for C in the key of C?
options: They share two notes, C and E
Am is the dominant of C
items.answer: They share two notes, C and E
items.why: Shared notes give vi a similar, home-like sound to I.
misconceptions: Forgets that C is a major chord
Confuses vi with the dominant
Confuses A with C as the root

items.q: A progression sounds most finished when it ends on:
items.why: The tonic is the stable home chord.
misconceptions: Believes the tension chord is the ending
Believes subdominant chords sound resolved
Believes the diminished chord sounds stable

items.q: Name the two dominant-function chords in a major key, as Roman numerals.
items.why: Both create tension that pulls back to I.

items.q: In G major, which chords have subdominant function? Name them by letter.
items.why: IV and ii are subdominant; in G they are C and Am.

lessons.title: Common Progressions and Writing Your Own
lessons.objective: Play classic progressions in any key and write an original progression using functions.
lessons.hook: A handful of progressions power thousands of songs, and learning why they work lets you write your own.
lessons.explain: I–IV–V–I moves home, away, tension, home: in G, G–C–D–G. I–V–vi–IV is the pop progression: in C, C–G–Am–F. ii–V–I is the strongest cadence, common in jazz: in C, Dm–G–C. To write your own, start on I, move through subdominant chords, reach V for tension, then resolve to I, or surprise the listener with vi.
key_facts: I–IV–V–I moves home, away, tension, home: in G, G–C–D–G.
I–V–vi–IV is the pop progression: in C, C–G–Am–F.
ii–V–I is the strongest cadence: in C, Dm–G–C.
To write your own, start on I, move through subdominant chords, reach V, then resolve to I or vi.

predict.q: In the pop progression C–G–Am–F, which chord is vi?

angles: Write the function map first, home → away → tension → home, then fill each slot with any chord of that function: I or vi, IV or ii, V or vii°.
Hear ii–V–I as a stronger version of IV–V–I: ii (Dm) shares two notes with IV (F), so it plays the same 'away' role with a smoother pull into V.

rungs.text: ii–V–I in G: ii is Am, V is D, I is G, so the progression is Am–D–G.
Write an 8-chord progression in D that starts on I, passes through ii or IV, reaches V, and ends on I.

claims: I–IV–V–I in G is G–C–D–G.
I–V–vi–IV in C is C–G–Am–F.
ii–V–I in C is Dm–G–C.
ii–V–I is widely used in jazz.

items.q: What is I–V–vi–IV in C?
items.why: In C, I is C, V is G, vi is Am and IV is F.
misconceptions: Believes vi is a major chord
Swaps the order of V and IV
Confuses vi with iii

items.q: What is ii–V–I in C?
items.why: ii is Dm, V is G, I is C.
misconceptions: Believes ii is major
Confuses V with IV
Confuses ii with iii

items.q: What is I–IV–V–I in G?
items.why: In G, IV is C and V is D.
misconceptions: Swaps IV and V
Confuses IV with ii
Confuses V with vi

items.q: In the key of C, which progression best follows the home–away–tension–home recipe?
items.why: It starts on I, goes to IV, reaches V and resolves to I.
misconceptions: Believes ending on ii resolves the progression
Believes tonic-group chords create tension
Believes a progression need not start or end at home

items.q: Write ii–V–I in D major.
items.why: In D, ii is Em, V is A, I is D.

items.q: Describe the recipe for writing your own progression using chord functions.
items.answer: Start on I, move through subdominant chords (IV or ii), reach V for tension, then resolve to I or surprise with vi.
items.why: This follows the natural pull of chord functions.

lessons.title: Moving a Progression to a New Key
lessons.objective: Transpose any progression to a new key using numerals or a capo.
lessons.hook: Transposing lets you fit any progression to your voice or to the chord shapes you play best.
lessons.explain: Transposing moves a progression to a new key while keeping its Roman numerals. Write the numerals, build the new key's chords, then swap them in. For example, C–Am–F–G is I–vi–IV–V. The chords of D major are D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°, so I–vi–IV–V becomes D–Bm–G–A. A capo transposes too: capo 2 with C shapes sounds in D, since each fret is a half step and C to D is two half steps.
key_facts: Transposing moves a progression to a new key while keeping its Roman numerals.
Write the numerals, build the new key's chords, then swap them in.
The chords of D major are D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°.
Capo 2 with C shapes sounds in D.
angles: Shift every chord root by the same distance: C to D is up a whole step, so Am goes to Bm, F to G and G to A, with each chord keeping its quality.
Think of the numerals as a recipe and the key as the kitchen: the recipe stays the same while the ingredients change.

rungs.text: G–Em–C–D to A: the numerals are I–vi–IV–V. A major chords: A, Bm, C#m, D, E, F#m, G#°. Result: A–F#m–D–E.
Transpose Am–F–C–G (vi–IV–I–V) from C to E major.

claims: Transposing preserves Roman numeral function.
D major's diatonic chords are D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°.
A capo on fret 2 raises pitch by two half steps.
I–vi–IV–V in D is D–Bm–G–A.

items.q: What stays the same when you transpose a progression?
items.why: Transposing changes the key but keeps each chord's degree.
misconceptions: Confuses transposing with replaying
Believes the bass note is fixed
Believes the capo defines the progression

items.q: In D major, the vi chord is:
items.why: B is the 6th degree of D, and vi is minor.
misconceptions: Believes vi is major
Confuses vi with ii
Confuses vi with iii

items.q: With a capo on fret 2, a G chord shape sounds as:
items.why: Two frets is two half steps, and G up a whole step is A.
misconceptions: Believes the capo raises only one half step
Believes fret 2 raises a major third
Believes a capo lowers pitch

items.q: C–G–Am–F transposed to G is:
items.why: I–V–vi–IV in G is G–D–Em–C.
misconceptions: Believes vi becomes major after transposing
Swaps the numerals during transposing
Believes IV becomes minor after transposing

items.q: List the seven chords of D major.
items.answer: D, Em, F#m, G, A, Bm, C#°
accept: D Em F#m G A Bm C#dim
items.why: Apply the major-key quality pattern to D E F# G A B C#.

items.q: What are the three steps for transposing with numerals?
items.answer: Write the numerals, build the new key's chords, then swap them in.
accept: find numerals, list new key's chords, replace
items.why: Numerals carry the progression into the new key.
